prime.problem: Graph searches, shortest paths, DP tables and number tricks look like 27 unrelated recipes. Learned that way, each one is a fact to memorise, and a new problem that doesn't match a recipe leaves you stuck. The course's real claim is that they are one move: name the states, name the moves, and make sure each state is handled once.
prime.fits: This is the map of course 3. It builds on the cost thinking of courses 1 and 2 (big-O, heaps, divide and conquer) and turns it on problems where the input is a set of states and moves rather than an array.
expect: a DAG as a fill order
five families: traverse, shortest path, DP, search, maths
prime.goal: Given a new problem, name its states and moves, estimate states × moves × cost, and pick the family (and card) that handles each state once.

attend: In T = states × moves × cost per move, which factor does each speedup row on this page shrink?
Why does naive fib(30) make 2,692,537 calls while the memo makes 59, when both explore the same 31 states?
What makes a relax step safe to apply in Dijkstra's order but not in an arbitrary order when weights can be negative?
Why is "every DP is a DAG" the same statement as "a table fill is a topological order"?
Which problems on the "when this advice doesn't apply" list fail because the state is a subset rather than a small tuple?

must: Name the state (node, cell, prefix pair, (day, trades)) → handle each state once → cost = states × moves × cost per move → the speedups come from cutting one of the three factors
A subproblem only needs smaller subproblems → the dependencies form a DAG → a fill order exists → DP; a cycle in the moves (four-way grid) → no fill order → search with BFS or Dijkstra instead

Shortest paths all apply one relax step → the order decides the cost: Dijkstra relaxes each edge once in distance order (needs weights ≥ 0), Bellman–Ford relaxes all edges each round (tolerates negatives) → about 8.0 × 10⁵ vs 5 × 10⁸ steps at V = 10⁴, E = 5 × 10⁴
The maths cards cut the step count itself → a remainder replaces repeated subtraction, one step per bit replaces one per unit → 10⁹ / 7 in 174 steps instead of 142,857,142
elevated: Python's recursion limit is 1,000 frames → any recursive DFS or top-down DP deeper than that raises RecursionError → that's why the cards prefer explicit stacks and bottom-up tables
reference: the method-per-job table (look it up when choosing)

compress.prompt: Draw the whole course's causal map from memory: one box for "states handled once" in the middle, the five families around it, and on each arrow the factor (states, moves or cost per move) that family cuts. Put at least one card name and one number on each family.
checklist: the centre: cost = states × moves × cost per move, each state handled once
traversal: visited sets / marking make each node O(1) → O(V + E)
shortest paths: relax in a safe order (Dijkstra) or in rounds (Bellman–Ford, Floyd)
DP: cache or table so each subproblem is solved once; the fill order is a topological order
search/backtracking: when the state is "everything chosen so far", nothing repeats, so prune instead
maths: fewer steps per answer (mod instead of subtract, one step per bit)

retrieve.q: Explain why a DP's running time is "states × work per state", using fib(30) and Coin Path as the two examples.
answer: each state is solved once and stored; later requests are O(1) lookups
Coin Path: n states × up to B options each = O(n·B)

retrieve.q: Walk through one relax step on the course's graph at the moment C has just been finalised with distance 2: which values change, and why can the old entry for B stay in the heap?
answer: heapq can't lower a key, so (3, B) is pushed and (4, B) stays
the stale (4, B) is skipped when popped because B is already final

retrieve.q: A problem's natural state is "which of the n items have been used so far". What does that do to the cost formula, and which tools are left when n = 40?
answer: states = 2ⁿ subsets, so DP over subsets is exponential (Hamiltonian path, 3-colouring are NP-complete)
for n around 20 subset DP can still work; at 40 it can't
what's left: backtracking with strong pruning, or a solver

compare.q: A graph search and a DP both "handle each state once". What is fundamentally different about how each one decides the order of states, and when does a DP problem have to be solved as a graph search instead?
answer: DP: the recurrence points only at smaller subproblems, so a fixed fill order (a topological order) exists
graph search: the order is discovered at run time (queue, stack or heap)
when moves can cycle (four-way grids, general graphs) there is no fill order, so you search: BFS, Dijkstra

compare.q: Bellman–Ford is described as a DP over paths. What is its state, what is the move, and which choice lets it handle negative weights that break Dijkstra?
answer: state: (node, at most r edges used)
move: extend by one edge (relax every edge each round)
it never finalises a node early, so a later negative edge can still lower a value
the price: O(V·E) instead of O((V + E) log V)

compare.q: Divide and conquer and DP both split a problem into smaller ones. Which property of the subproblems decides whether a cache helps, and what does the cache cost when it doesn't help?
answer: DP needs overlapping subproblems; merge sort's halves are disjoint and never repeat
with no repeats, a cache only adds memory and lookups
with repeats (fib), the cache turns exponential calls into one per state

predict.q: You add a fourth factor to the formula: some problems ask for every solution rather than the best one. Predict what happens to the "handle each state once" savings for Decode Ways on '*' × 10⁵ if you must list the decodings instead of counting them.
predict.answer: The savings vanish. Counting keeps three numbers per position, O(n), because the DP merges all ways that reach the same state into one count. Listing has to output every decoding, and the count is a 101,859-digit number, so the output alone is exponential. No cache can make writing the answers cheaper; this is why listing problems (Expression Add Operators) use backtracking.

apply.task: Classify four problems without solving them. For each, write the state, the moves, the family and a cost estimate: (1) edit distance between two 1,000-character strings; (2) fewest moves for a knight between two squares on an 8 × 8 board; (3) number of ways to climb 10 stairs taking 1, 2 or 3 steps; (4) whether a set of course prerequisites contains a cycle.
apply.done: You have (1) state (i, j), 1,001 × 1,001 = 1,002,001 states, 3 moves each, DP; (2) state = square, 64 states, up to 8 moves, BFS; (3) state = stairs left, 11 states, 3 moves, DP (answer 274); (4) state = course, Kahn's algorithm in O(V + E).
apply.hint: Ask for each: do the moves only go to smaller subproblems (DP), or can they cycle (search)? Are all moves the same cost (BFS)?

reflect: Which family did you put a problem in and then have to move it? What gave it away?
Could you explain, without naming an algorithm, why handling each state once is the whole trick?
Which prediction did you get wrong: the listing blow-up, or the DAG/no-DAG split?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: state choice → cost, or move order → correctness (Dijkstra vs Bellman–Ford)?
Which family will you study first, and which card in it do you expect to find hardest?
